title: Explaining Rankings with Hidden Group Bonuses

problem.claim: Determine a linear utility function that correlates with observed candidate rankings.

gap.claim: Traditional ranking explanation models assume full visibility into the feature sets determining utility scores, despite sensitive attributes sometimes being hidden or partially observed and influencing outcomes through additive group bonuses.

contributions.claim: Studies ranking explanation when sensitive features are unobserved but may influence rankings through group-specific linear boosts.

narrative_sequence.summary: Linear utility functions correlated with observed candidate rankings are foundational for several applications.
Traditional models assume complete visibility into the features used for utility scoring.
Sensitive attributes may be hidden or partially observed while affecting outcomes through additive fairness-oriented bonuses.
The paper studies ranking explanation with unobserved sensitive features and group-specific linear boosts.

source_observation.claim: Ranking explanations may need to account for hidden sensitive attributes that affect outcomes through group-specific additive boosts.

interpretation.claim: Explanatory models based only on visible features can be incomplete when group-dependent effects influence rankings.

application.claim: When explaining rankings in settings such as admissions, hiring, or recommendation, model hidden or partially observed group effects as a possible source of ranking behavior.

exception.claim: The supplied abstract units do not establish whether hidden group effects are present in a particular deployment or how accurately they can be recovered.

unknowns: No experiments, datasets, algorithms, theoretical results, or quantitative findings are supplied.
The abstract does not specify how sensitive groups or group-specific boosts are identified.
The abstract does not report limitations, comparative baselines, or independent verification.
